name: relational-categorization
title: Relational Categorization — Memory in Embodied Dynamics (Williams, Beer & Gasser 2008)
lead:
This is the MEMORY model of the set. The other agents react to a present
stimulus; this one must remember. It sees object 1, which falls away, waits
through a blank interval, then sees object 2 and must act on how the two
COMPARE. Because object 1 is absent during the decision, any relational
behaviour is direct evidence that its size is carried in neural state. The
scientific interest is the memory trace itself: how the first object is
encoded, held, and read out.

at_a_glance.role: the agent catches the larger / avoids the smaller, above the memoryless ceiling
object 1's size is encoded in and held by neural state across the ISI

glossary.definition: Classifying a stimulus by its relation to another (here: object 2's size relative to object 1), not by any absolute property.
Holding information briefly for use in an imminent decision — here, object 1's size across the inter-stimulus interval, realized as CTRNN state.
The blank interval between object 1 disappearing and object 2 appearing, during which nothing is sensed, so any retained information is memory.
The best accuracy a policy that reads only the current object (ignoring object 1) can reach on the battery — here ~0.625; beating it requires memory.
A sensor casting a ray that returns the distance to an object it hits; the array of rays gives the object's angular 'shadow', from which size is perceptible.

biological_story:
Comparison needs memory. To judge whether this fruit is bigger than the last
one, an animal must carry the last one in its head — the two are never present
together. Williams, Beer & Gasser asked whether the smallest kind of nervous
system could do that: not store a number in a labelled slot, but hold the past
in the ongoing activity of a few continuously-interacting neurons. The agent
here does exactly that. It watches the first object fall, and the shape of its
neural activity shifts in a way that tracks that object's size. The object
vanishes; the activity holds its imprint through the blank interval — a memory,
visible as a flat trace that remembers. When the second object falls, the
network's response depends on this held value as well as on what it now sees,
and the agent moves to intercept the larger object or to let the smaller one
pass. It does not always get it right — reading the memory out into the right
movement is the hard part — but the remembering itself is unmistakable.
question:
Can a small continuous-time recurrent neural network categorize an object by
its size RELATIVE to a previously-seen one — catching the second of two
sequentially-presented objects when it is larger, avoiding it when smaller —
given that the first object is gone by the time the second appears, so the
comparison can only be made through internal memory?
hypothesis:
An agent evolved for this relative-size task will hold a trace of the first
object's size in its CTRNN state across the inter-stimulus interval and read it
out when the second object arrives, producing a relational decision with no
dedicated memory store — memory as a property of the coupled brain-body-
environment dynamics, the point of Williams, Beer & Gasser (2008).

executive.what_is_this:
An evolved 8-neuron CTRNN driving a horizontal catcher with ray distance-
sensors (the shared categorical-perception body) in a world where two
circles fall in sequence. It catches the second circle if it is larger than
the first and avoids it if smaller. The genome (CTRNN + sensor weights) was
evolved by the workspace's own GA and committed; the studies replay it
deterministically.
executive.verdict:
Reproduced (honest partial). The evolved agent genuinely holds the first
object in memory: during the inter-stimulus interval, with no object present,
its neural state encodes object 1's size with correlation 0.88. It uses that
trace to categorize relationally, reaching 0.69 accuracy — above the 0.625
ceiling that ANY memoryless (single-object) policy can reach on this battery,
and above the 0.5 always-catch/always-avoid baselines. The memory is clean;
the decision read-out is imperfect, so accuracy is modest.
executive.verdict_detail:
From the committed seed (8-neuron CTRNN, pop 130, gen 220, seed 0), verified
in the test suite: accuracy > the 0.625 memoryless ceiling (achieved 0.688)
on BOTH relations (catch 0.625, avoid 0.75, not by always-catching or
always-avoiding), and the ISI neural state correlates > 0.80 with object 1's
size (achieved 0.88 during the real moving-body trial; ~0.95 with the body
held fixed). The battery is role-balanced per size so that no
absolute-size threshold exceeds ~0.625 — the above-ceiling accuracy therefore
REQUIRES using object 1 relative to object 2, i.e. memory. Honest scope +
tuning: evolving robust relative-size memory is hard. A first attempt with an
asymmetric reward collapsed to always-avoiding; a SYMMETRIC accuracy-aligned
reward (always-catch and always-avoid both score exactly 0.5) and a larger
net (8 neurons) were needed. The clean memory trace (0.88) with only modest
accuracy (0.69) locates the bottleneck in the decision read-out, not the
memory.

decisions_needed.question: Push for higher accuracy (bigger net / much more evolution), or report this as the honest minimal result (clean memory, imperfect read-out)?
decisions_needed.context: The memory encoding is already strong (corr 0.88); further gains are in the sensorimotor decision, which costs substantial additional evolution.

scientific_argument.main_claim:
Relational categorization here rests on working memory realized as CTRNN
dynamics: the first object's size is written into neural state, persists
through a stimulus-free interval, and is read out against the second object —
with no dedicated memory module. The agent beats every memoryless policy
precisely because it remembers.
evidence_for: The ISI neural state (object absent) encodes object 1's size with correlation 0.88 (figures/memory_dynamics.png).
Accuracy 0.688 exceeds the 0.625 memoryless-threshold ceiling AND the 0.5 always-catch/always-avoid baselines, on both relations (catch 0.625, avoid 0.75).
The battery is role-balanced per size, so no absolute-size (single-object) policy can exceed ~0.625 — above-ceiling accuracy requires memory of object 1.
The learned decision map tracks the s2>s1 diagonal (figures/decision_map.png), the relational boundary.
evidence_against: Accuracy is modest (0.688, ~11/16): the clean memory is not fully exploited by the sensorimotor read-out, so the agent still mis-categorizes some pairs.
key_figures: figures/memory_dynamics.png — object 1's size held in neural state over the ISI (the memory trace)
figures/relational.gif — the two objects in sequence and the catch/avoid outcome
figures/decision_map.png — the learned relational decision boundary vs the s2=s1 diagonal
figures/neural_activity.gif — the CTRNN across the two phases + ISI, the memory trace persisting
caveats: Fitness used a symmetric accuracy-aligned reward (fixed policies score 0.5); the shaping is a documented design choice.
Clean-room constants (8-neuron CTRNN, catch_radius 3.0, ISI 40 steps, sizes 2-6 with adjacent |Δ|=1 pairs): documented choices, not Williams-Beer-Gasser-exact.
Honest partial: the memory is clean (corr 0.88) but the decision read-out is imperfect (accuracy 0.69).

studies.name: relative-size-discrimination
studies.title: Catch the Larger, Avoid the Smaller
studies.question:
Does the evolved agent catch the second object when it is larger than the
first and avoid it when smaller — above what any memoryless policy can do?

findings.summary: Accuracy 0.688 (catch 0.625, avoid 0.75) — above the 0.625 memoryless ceiling and the 0.5 fixed-policy baselines; a genuine but imperfect relational categorizer.
findings.detail:
figures/relational.gif shows a should-catch and a should-avoid trial and the
outcome; figures/decision_map.png shows the learned response over the (s1,s2)
plane tracking the s2=s1 diagonal (imperfectly).

studies.claim:
The agent categorizes by RELATIVE size, reaching 0.688 accuracy (catch 0.625,
avoid 0.75) — above the 0.625 ceiling that any single-object (memoryless)
policy can reach on this role-balanced battery, and above the 0.5 always-catch
/ always-avoid baselines.

derived.insight: Accuracy 0.688 (catch 0.625, avoid 0.75) — above the 0.625 memoryless ceiling and the 0.5 fixed-policy baselines; a genuine but imperfect relational categorizer.

studies.name: memory-dynamics
studies.title: Object 1 Held in Memory
studies.question:
Is the first object's size actually held in the CTRNN's state across the
inter-stimulus interval, when no object is present — i.e. is this real memory?

findings.summary: ISI neural state correlates 0.88 with object 1's size — object 1 is clearly held in persistent memory across the stimulus-free interval.
findings.detail:
figures/memory_dynamics.png shows the mid-ISI activation rising monotonically
with s1 (corr 0.88) and the trace persisting flat through the ISI;
figures/neural_activity.gif shows the memory trace holding across the phase1 |
ISI | phase2 raster.

studies.claim:
Yes. During the ISI (object absent), the agent's neural state encodes object
1's size with correlation 0.88: the trace is set while object 1 falls and
persists through the blank interval until object 2 arrives. Memory realized as
CTRNN dynamics, not a stored value.

derived.insight: ISI neural state correlates 0.88 with object 1's size — object 1 is clearly held in persistent memory across the stimulus-free interval.
